definition: Artificial reproduction is the re-creation of life brought about by means other than natural ones.
details: It is new life built by human plans and projects. Examples include artificial selection, artificial insemination, in vitro fertilization, artificial womb, artificial cloning, and kinematic replication. Artificial reproduction is one aspect of artificial life. Artificial reproduction can be categorized into one of two classes according to its capacity to be self-sufficient: non-assisted reproductive technology and assisted reproductive technology. Cutting plants' stems and placing them in compost is a form of assisted artificial reproduction, xenobots are an example of a more autonomous type of reproduction, while the artificial womb presented in the movie the Matrix illustrates a non assisted hypothetical technology. The idea of artificial reproduction has led to various technologies.

explainer.lead: Artificial reproduction means creating new life through human-designed methods rather than natural reproduction alone. It covers techniques as different as plant cuttings, in vitro fertilization and self-replicating xenobots, making it a broad concept within artificial life.

tiers.eli5: Usually, living things make new living things without people planning each step. Artificial reproduction is like taking a stem from a plant and putting it in compost so it can grow into a new plant: a person helps start the process. Some methods need that help, while others can reproduce more on their own.
tiers.practitioner: In practice, the method and its degree of self-sufficiency are the key distinctions. Human-guided cases include plant propagation, artificial insemination and in vitro fertilization, while xenobots illustrate a more autonomous form. Avoid treating all techniques as equally autonomous or hypothetical systems, such as the artificial womb in The Matrix, as available technology.
tiers.paperLevel: Artificial reproduction is the recreation of life through means other than natural ones and constitutes one aspect of artificial life. Its methods can be classified by their capacity for self-sufficiency as assisted or non-assisted reproductive technology. Examples range from human-assisted plant propagation to kinematic replication, with hypothetical systems requiring separate treatment from demonstrated cases.

explainer.example: A person cuts stems from a plant and places them in compost so they can produce new plants. Because human action establishes the reproduction process, this is assisted artificial reproduction.

explainer.intuition: The central idea is that new life results from human plans and projects rather than natural reproduction alone. The concept includes both methods that depend on human assistance and methods capable of greater self-sufficiency.
howItWorks: A human-designed method replaces or assists a natural reproductive process.
The method may involve selection, insemination, fertilization, cloning, propagation or replication.
New life or a new self-replicating entity results.
The method is classified by how self-sufficient the reproduction is.
explainer.whyItMatters: It provides a common framework for technologies ranging from artificial selection and in vitro fertilization to artificial cloning and artificial wombs. The self-sufficiency distinction also helps separate human-assisted techniques from more autonomous reproduction.
misconceptions: It is not limited to human fertility treatments; plant propagation and artificial-life systems also qualify.
Not every method requires continuing human assistance.
The artificial womb shown in The Matrix is hypothetical, not an established technology.
